newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Switzerland's CS takes big charge, sees loss.
newsitem.headline: Switzerland's CS takes big charge, sees loss.

text.p: CS Holding said Friday it would take a 3.9 billion Swiss franc ($2.9 billion) restructuring charge and post a loss this year, the latest of the country's big banks to be hurt by the weak Swiss economy.

The banking and financial services company, which announced a major restructuring in July, said the charge would include setting aside extraordinary reserves and provisions against credit losses, as well as depreciation.

As a result, CS Holding, which owns a majority stake in CS First Boston Corp., the American investment bank, said it expected a 1996 loss of about 2.1 billion francs ($1.6 billion) compared with a 1995 profit of 1.54 billion ($1.1 billion).
Despite the expected loss, CS Holding will maintain its the dividend at 1995 levels of four francs ($2.98) a share.
CS said it was moving away from making provisions for actual defaults to setting aside funds for statistically expected credit losses.
The move follows a similar step taken by rival Swiss Bank Corp. in September. SBC was the first Swiss bank to adopt such a method of calculating loss provisions.
Swiss banks have been suffering from high loan-loss provisions and credit losses in their domestic business as a result of the sharp and lasting downturn in the Swiss economy.
Analysts had expected the CS Holding move in view of the dire loan situation in the domestic sector.
"A cleaning out is something I always wanted to see," said James Hyde at Merrill Lynch in London.
"If they hadn't done anything this year, the comparisons next year would be bad," said Zuercher Kantonalbank analyst Christof Bieri in referring to comparisons to other big banks in Switzerland.
As part of its restructuring, SBC is taking write-offs totalling 3.3 billion francs ($2.5 billion) this year, a step that will result in an estimated 1996 loss of 1.9 billion francs ($1.4 billion).

Union Bank of Switzerland, while not revamping its provisioning methods, is taking a 3 billion franc ($2.2 billion) charge to cover credit risk and restructuring. It expects to lose about 500 million francs ($372 million) this year.
The CS announcement outlining the measures was generally viewed as positive, but some analysts said there were still some unanswered questions.

"It remains to be seen if this is enough," said Kleinwort Benson analyst James Alexander. He said that before making a final determination, analysts would have to see more details on the group's troubled loans.

Separately, CS Holding said a consortium comprising German energy companies Bayernwerk, Badenwerk and Energieversorgung Schwaben, Swiss utility Nordostschweizerische Kraftwerke and CS Holding will take over CS Holding's current stake in newly formed Watt AG, a company formed to hold CS Holding's utility interests.
